script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight's story is The Bee with the Mail Bag, told by Hettie Moss, who keeps hives at the edge of Larkspur Woods. Get comfortable, find the warmest corner of the room, and let the evening go slowly.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Painted Hive]]

Come in and sit on the upturned crate by the shed door. It is the best seat, and the only one. I have a little honey in a jar and a spoon, if you want it. Now, you will have noticed it on your way up the path. Why does one beehive at the edge of Larkspur Woods have a painting of a bee delivering the mail? The bee wears a little cap and carries a satchel, and it is handing a letter to a surprised foxglove. Everyone who walks past asks me. I always say it is not my hive and not my painting, and then I tell them the whole story, which is why it takes so long to get anywhere with me.

[pause]

The hive belongs to Orrin Birch. He carried the post around Fernwick for forty-one years, on foot and by bicycle, in every weather the coast could think of. Last spring he retired, and he bought one hive and a book on beekeeping, and he asked if he might keep the hive beside mine. Tonight, in the middle of October, he is painting the front board for the very first time, in the lamplight of his little shed.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER Where the Idea Came From]]

I ought to tell you where the idea came from. There is a country called Slovenia, up in the mountains of central Europe, and for a couple of hundred years its beekeepers painted the front boards of their hives. Not a stripe or a name, mind you, but whole little pictures, as bright as the covers of old storybooks. There are hunters and hares, and tailors riding goats, and a woman scolding a wolf for being late. Some are proverbs and some are only jokes. Thousands of different pictures were painted, and no two villages told quite the same ones.

[pause]

In those mountain villages, the hives were kept in long wooden bee houses, stacked in rows like the drawers of a tall cabinet, so that all the painted boards faced outward in a bright patchwork. A traveler walking past would see a whole village's humor at once: a fox playing the fiddle on one door, a cobbler losing his shoe to a goose on the next. The custom faded as hives grew plain and metal, but in recent years people have started painting them again, and I think that is the best news I have heard about beekeeping in a decade.

[pause]

The people there say the pictures helped the bees find their own door. A hive in a long row of hives looks very much like all the others, and a bee coming home in the dusk is in a hurry. A painting of a blue hunter and a red hare is much easier to recognize than a plain plank. I do not know whether that is true. I have never met a bee who would say. But I know that the pictures made the beekeepers laugh, and that is a good enough reason to paint almost anything.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Lamplight and Paint]]

There is a reason Orrin chose the bee and the mail. For all forty-one years of his route, my gate was the sixth stop on Larkspur Lane, and every June, a single bee would sit on my letter box and refuse to move. Orrin would stand there with the post in his hand, politely waiting, and say good morning to it. He used to tell me that the bees took the mail more seriously than most of the neighbors. I think he decided, years ago, that one day he would give one of them a proper job.

[pause]

Orrin found a photograph of one of those boards in a library book, and he carried it up to the shed in his coat pocket. The shed smells of beeswax, cedar shavings and warm tin. A lantern hangs from a nail in the beam, and its flame is the color of the inside of a pear. On the workbench sit seven small pots of paint, the board laid flat on two bricks, and a jam jar of water that has gone slightly blue.

[pause]

The shed has other things in it, all of them in the soft brown shadows. There is a smoker with a leather bellows, hung from a hook. There are stacks of empty wooden frames, a veil on a nail, and shelves of honey jars with handwritten labels, the writing so neat that I can only assume it was the postman's. A small iron stove in the corner has been lit for the evening, and it ticks quietly as it warms the cedar shavings on the floor.

[pause]

The board itself is a plain piece of pine, about the size of a large loaf of bread. Orrin sanded it this afternoon until it was as smooth as a stream stone, and he has already brushed on a coat of cream-colored paint, which smells of linseed oil and has dried to a soft matte glow. He sits down on a stool, rolls his sleeves to the elbow, and picks up the thinnest brush.

[pause]

He mixes the colors first, on a chipped white saucer. A little yellow ochre for the body of the bee, and a drop of burnt brown for the bands. A smear of ultramarine blue, thinned with water until it is the shade of a morning window. The paint has the cool, slightly chalky smell of a school art room, and his brushes, which have soft squirrel-hair tips, lie in a neat row on a folded cloth, arranged from the thickest to the finest.

[pause]

He begins with the bee. He is not a quick painter. He holds the brush the way he used to hold a pen when he wrote out addresses, with his tongue between his teeth, and every stroke is laid down as carefully as a letter into a box. The body is a golden yellow, with two bands of brown, and it takes a good while. Then comes a pair of pale blue wings, so thin that they are really only suggestions.

[long pause]

Then the cap. It is the postman's cap, of course, dark blue with a little peak and a tiny brass button, and Orrin paints it a shade too large, so that it slips down over one of the bee's eyes. He looks at it for a moment and decides to leave it. A mail carrier who cannot quite see where he is going is, he says later, a very true picture of the trade.

[pause]

The satchel is brown, with a strap across the chest and a flap held down by two stitches of red. He paints the letter in the bee's hand, white with a dark corner for the stamp. The foxglove takes longer, because foxgloves have so many small bells on one stalk. He paints each one a slightly different shade of plum, and a pale freckled throat inside, and the whole stalk leans a little toward the bee, as if it has been waiting all year for news.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Quiet Hives]]

Outside, the evening has gone cold and still. The pines make their long, low murmur, and somewhere beneath them a stream is running over stones. The hives stand in a row at the edge of the clearing, two of them, a shape of pale wood against the dark. Inside, the bees have drawn together into a warm ball for the winter, and the only sound is a faint, contented hum, like a kettle thinking about boiling.

[pause]

I give the nearest hive a gentle pat as I go past, the way you might pat the flank of a sleeping horse. The wood under my palm is cool on the outside, but if I hold my hand there long enough, I can feel the faintest warmth coming through, from thousands of small bodies pressed close together. I tuck a folded sack of dry straw on top of each roof against the frost, and I check that the little entrances are narrow enough to keep out the drafts.

[pause]

I come down the path with a cup of tea for Orrin, and stand in the doorway. He does not notice me. The lantern flame leans and settles. The painted foxglove is almost done, and the little bee, in its slipping cap, looks quietly pleased with itself. Orrin lays down the brush, wipes his fingers on a rag, and sits back with a long, slow sigh.

[pause]

"It will dry by morning," he says. I put the tea down beside the paint pots. He does not drink it. His hands are in his lap, and his eyes are closing, and the lantern glow has made his gray hair look like warm straw. I pull the old green wool blanket from the hook by the door and lay it over his shoulders. He murmurs something about the second-class post, and then he is asleep.

[long pause]

Outside, the pines go on with their murmuring. The stream goes on. The lantern burns low and steady on its nail, and on the workbench the little bee delivers its letter, over and over, to a flower that has been waiting all year. Tomorrow the board will go on the hive. For tonight, it rests on its two bricks in the light, drying slowly, the color of honey and cream.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Why does one beehive have a painted bee delivering the mail? Because Orrin Birch carried the post for forty-one years.

[pause]

In Slovenia, beekeepers painted their hive boards with hunters and hares and jokes. Orrin paints a bee in a postman's cap.

[long pause]

The shed is warm. The lantern is low. The paint is cream and gold and plum.

[pause]

The bee has a satchel. The flower is waiting. The letter is delivered.

[long pause]

Orrin sits back. His eyes close. The blanket is green, and the hives are quiet.

[long pause]

And that is the story of the bee with the mail bag. There is still honey in the jar, and the crate is yours until morning. The woods can wait. Good night.
